analogies: Compound interest is like a snowball rolling downhill — it starts small, but gathers mass and speed the longer it rolls.
Exponential growth is like folding a piece of paper: after 42 folds, the stack would reach the moon.
Think of compounding as a copy machine that copies its own copies — the stack doubles every cycle.
Churn is a leaky bucket — pouring in more leads will never outrun the holes at the bottom.
Losing customers is like trying to fill a bath with the drain open. Fix the drain before you turn on the tap.
Retention is the foundation of a building. You can add floors indefinitely, but not if the ground floor is crumbling.
Product-market fit is like a key in a lock — you know immediately when it clicks.
Before product-market fit, growth is like pushing a boulder uphill. After it, you're steering a boulder downhill.
Finding product-market fit is less like aiming and more like listening — the market tells you where the fit is.
Technical debt is like financial debt — useful in the short term, but the interest compounds and eventually crowds out everything else.
Shipping code without refactoring is like paving over a pothole. You'll drive over it fine today, but the road will buckle.
Technical debt is the engineering equivalent of tidying a room by stuffing everything in the closet. The closet will eventually explode.
Unit economics are the heartbeat of a business. You can look healthy on the outside and still be losing money on every transaction.
Selling below cost and hoping to make it up on volume is like driving faster when you're lost — you get further from the destination, just more quickly.
A positive unit margin is the engine. Everything else — marketing, headcount, expansion — is just the vehicle.
Network effects are like a telephone — one phone is useless, two is a conversation, a million is infrastructure.
A marketplace with network effects is like a coral reef: slow to grow, but once it reaches critical mass, everything else attaches itself.
Network effects create a gravitational field. The more mass you accumulate, the more you attract.
Cash flow is the oxygen of a business. You can be profitable on paper and still suffocate if it runs out.
Runway is like the fuel gauge on a long drive through the desert — the number that matters most isn't how far you've come, it's how much is left.
Managing burn rate is like rationing water on a hike: you adjust your pace to reach the next water source, not to reach the destination faster.
Payroll compliance is a building's fire code: invisible until the day it saves you — or burns you.
Ignoring payroll regulation is like ignoring a slow oil leak in your car. The engine runs fine until suddenly it doesn't.
Compliance is the foundation, not the ceiling. You don't build on sand and then wonder why the walls crack.
An API is the electrical socket in a wall — we don't think about the infrastructure behind it, just that anything with a plug can connect.
Our API is the plumbing — nobody admires it until it leaks.
Integrations are like roads between cities: they unlock value that couldn't exist in isolation.
Data without insight is a library without a catalogue — the answers are in there, but no one can find them.
Raw data is like ore. Insight is the refined metal. Most companies are still mining; few are refining.
Analytics is the rearview mirror. Strategy is the windscreen. You need both, but only one tells you where you're going.
Onboarding is a first date, not a wedding. Don't ask for everything up front.
A great onboarding experience is like a warm welcome at a hotel — the first impression sets the tone for every stay that follows.
Onboarding is the bridge between a user's intent and their first moment of value. If the bridge is shaky, most people turn back.
LTV is the total value of a fruit tree, not just this season's harvest. You plant it, tend it, and it pays back for years.
Judging customers by their first purchase is like judging a restaurant by its bread basket. The real value comes later.
LTV is the lens that turns short-term acquisition cost into a long-term investment.
A moat is the set of reasons a competitor can't simply copy you, even if they can see exactly what you're doing.
Data network effects are like the Grand Canyon — impressive today, but what matters is that they took millions of years to form.
Brand is a moat built from trust. Once established, competitors can spend fortunes and not cross it.
Organisational change is like replacing the engines on a plane mid-flight — the business must keep running as you transform it.
Change without communication is like moving the furniture at night. People know something shifted, they just keep stubbing their toes.
Resistance to change is like a rubber band — pull too fast and it snaps; apply consistent steady pressure and it stretches.
A flat structure is like open-plan seating — great for collaboration, but exhausting when everyone can interrupt everyone.
Hierarchy is scaffolding, not the building itself. You need it to construct something, but the goal is eventually to remove it.
Span of control is like a branch on a tree — it can only hold so much weight before it bends or breaks.
Strategy without execution is a map without a vehicle — it shows where to go, but doesn't move you.
A brilliant strategy poorly executed is like a perfect recipe with no chef. The dish never arrives.
Execution is the tax you pay on strategy. The higher your ambition, the heavier the tax.
Scaling operations is like turning a speedboat into a cargo ship: you gain capacity, but you need a much longer runway to manoeuvre.
Scaling is not just doing more of the same — it's rebuilding the factory floor while the orders keep coming in.
Operational scale is like compound interest in reverse for complexity: every new layer adds friction that compounds over time.
Switching vendors is repotting a plant — stressful for a week, then it grows.
High switching costs are like being in a lease: you knew the terms when you signed, but leaving still costs you.
Vendor lock-in is gravity. You don't notice it until you try to leave, then you feel every pound.
Digital transformation is renovating a building while people are still working in it — modernisation without disruption.
Transforming a legacy system is like rewiring a house without turning off the electricity. Possible, but it demands extreme care.
Digital transformation isn't a project with an end date — it's a shift in how the organisation breathes.
Brand is a promise you make and a promise you keep — the gap between the two is where trust lives or dies.
Reputation is like porcelain: decades to build, a moment to shatter, and never quite the same after repair.
Your brand is what people say about you when you're not in the room.
A sales funnel is like panning for gold — you need a lot of water and gravel to find a few nuggets.
The pipeline is a river: it looks fine on the surface, but without upstream rain, it dries up months later.
Closing a deal is like landing a plane — most of the work happened miles before touchdown.
A roadmap is a hypothesis, not a contract. The best teams treat it like a weather forecast — directionally right, updated constantly.
Prioritising features is like packing a suitcase for a trip you haven't planned yet. Everyone wants to bring more than fits.
The roadmap is the menu, not the meal. What gets built is what gets served.
Risk management is not about avoiding risk — it's about choosing which risks to carry intentionally.
Unmitigated risk is like driving without insurance. You might be fine, but a single event changes everything.
Scenario planning is like packing an umbrella — you don't expect rain, but you'd rather have it and not need it.
Culture is what happens when no one is watching. The real values of an organisation show up in the small decisions.
Culture is like a river: it carves its own path over time. You can redirect it, but you can't stop it from flowing.
Hiring for culture fit without culture add is like only eating the foods you already know — safe, but the menu never grows.
Leadership is less about having the answers and more about creating the conditions for others to find them.
Delegation without trust is like lending your car and driving alongside to make sure they don't crash.
A leader's job is to turn the lights on, not to illuminate every corner themselves.
Innovation is like prospecting — you dig a lot of holes before you strike something valuable.
An A/B test is a small, controlled argument with reality. Reality always wins.
Running experiments is like placing small bets. You want to lose cheaply and often enough to find the bet worth doubling down on.
Market timing is surfing — being too early is as bad as being too late. You need to catch the wave, not the trough.
A great idea in the wrong decade is just an idea. Timing is the silent co-founder every startup either has or doesn't.
Being early to a market is like planting a flag on land you can't yet settle. Someone else arrives when the conditions are right.
Raising money is like dating — you want to find someone who believes in the same future you do, not just someone who'll say yes.
Investors are buying a ticket on the plane before it takes off — they're betting on the destination, not just the current altitude.
Due diligence is like a medical check-up before a marathon. The investor wants to know you can finish the race.
Attribution is like asking which raindrop caused the flood — every one contributed, and singling one out misses the point.
Last-click attribution is like giving the finisher's medal to the person who tied your shoes at the finish line.
Multi-touch attribution is the honest map of how a customer actually reached you — messier than the straight line we'd prefer.
Great hiring is like casting a film — skills are important, but chemistry and timing make or break the final product.
A high performer in the wrong role is like a concert pianist asked to tune the piano. Talent wasted on the wrong problem.
Slow hiring, fast firing is wisdom. The inverse is how most bad teams are built.
